newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarians face winter of poverty.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarians face winter of poverty.

text.p: A ragged group of scavengers armed with wire hooks and plastic sacks digs over the morning's delivery at a vast rubbish tip on the edge of the Bulgarian capital.
As garbage trucks trundle through the mud to discharge the capital's waste, families dodge bulldozers levelling the ground in scenes more reminiscent of Africa than Europe.
For the past year or so, as Bulgaria's economic crisis worsens, up to 200 people have been scratching a living by gathering waste paper and drink cans on the Dolny Bogrov dump.
Metodi Boichev, 17, who has been working there for the past month, said even the rubbish was deteriorating. "People don't even have garbage any more because of the crisis," he said.

Yordan Atanasov, 34, who lives with his wife in one of the scavengers' shacks on the edge of the dump, said he made about 500 levs (about $1.40) on a good day. "It's enough for bread, nothing more," he said.

Boichev said he quit school and went to Germany to look for work, returning after a month to find there were no jobs in Bulgaria either. "When I came back from Germany I saw that people had lost all hope," he said.

Stefka Valentinova, a beaming green-eyed 10-year-old in blue and yellow wellington boots and a headscarf, said she and her parents gathered paper from early morning until dusk, took it to be weighed, then went to a nearby village to spend their earnings on bread.
Seven years after communist leader Todor Zhivkov was removed from power, the poorest Bulgarians are not the only ones still waiting to see some concrete benefit from reform.

"Bulgarians are still relying on things they had before 1990 -- their cars, apartments, the land they work on -- some people are still wearing clothes they've had since before 1990," said Deputy Social Care Minister Evgeniya Spasova.
She said her ministry was supporting with welfare payments about 20 percent of the population regarded as living in absolute poverty.
"Poverty will rise further in the next year if we don't take serious steps to revive the economy and the agricultural sector, for which we need serious foreign investment."
By the time the rubbish reaches Dolny Bogrov, there is not much left. Dustbins in Sofia's more prosperous areas are subject to nightly scrutiny by scavengers.
City markets are full of people, but not many are buying. Sofia woke on Monday to its first snow of the winter, but many people are struggling to pay heating bills.
An average state wage is 10,000 levs a month, though private businesses pay 20,000 or 30,000.
Elderly people living on fixed pensions are particularly hard hit by soaring inflation and the lev has collapsed from 70 to the dollar at the start of the year to 360 on Friday.
After a flood of requests for heating to be turned off or radiators removed altogether, the government promised to not to increase heating prices through the winter.
The Health Ministry says poverty-related illnesses such as tuberculosis are on the increase and the number of babies with low birth weight, another indicator of poverty, has risen.
"The most worrying thing is that cases of tuberculosis among young people are increasing," said Deputy Health Minister Tanya Cholakova.

President Zhelyu Zhelev warned on Thursday that a strict monetary regime proposed by the International Monetary Fund and expected to be introduced early next year was Bulgaria's last chance to pull itself out of the crisis caused by seven years of delayed reforms.
"If we miss that chance...this failure will pursue us into the next century," he said.
